listenings.text: I have sat in the middle of a lot of arguments that started as a misunderstanding, and almost all of them started in the same place. Somebody left a meeting and told a colleague what had been agreed, and the version that got written down was not the version that was said. Not a lie. Just a translation. Somebody says we are open to a September closing, and by the time it reaches the finance team it has become they committed to September. Two verbs of difference, and now one side believes there is a commitment and the other side does not know it made one. So my rule with clients is simple and it is not about honesty, it is about mechanics. Whoever writes the recap owns the deal, because everything anybody remembers three weeks later comes out of that email and not out of the room. If you were in the meeting and you do not write the recap, you have handed the memory of it to somebody else.

There is a habit I try to break in every founder I advise, and it is not a language problem, it is a confidence problem that shows up as a language problem. When they report what the other side said, they soften it. The buyer says your margin is too thin for this multiple, and the founder tells his own board that the buyer had some questions about the numbers. He has just deleted the objection. Now his board cannot help him, because they do not know what was actually said, and he will walk into the next meeting alone with a problem nobody else has heard. Report the sentence, not your feeling about the sentence. If the buyer said the margin was too thin, say he said the margin was too thin. You are allowed to disagree with it in the very next sentence. What you are not allowed to do is edit it on the way home.
